title: The state machine
sub: What the compiler folds all of a method's awaits into
cards/0/title: await isn't magic, it's a switch
cards/0/body:
The compiler rewrites an async method into a struct: a state machine. Local variables become its fields, the method body becomes a MoveNext function, and the step number lives in a state field. Every await is a spot where MoveNext can return and later come back. Next to it sits the builder (AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<T>), a helper that creates the method's task and completes it.

What happens when SumAsync is called (code below):

  • 1. The struct is created with state = -1, meaning "just started".
  • 2. builder.Start calls the first MoveNext right away, synchronously, on the caller's thread. That's why a method runs like an ordinary one up to its first await.
  • 3. MoveNext hits an awaiter that isn't done: it writes the step number to state, subscribes itself through builder.AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted (which uses the awaiter's UnsafeOnCompleted inside) and returns.
  • 4. SumAsync returns builder.Task, a task that isn't complete yet.
  • 5. The GetAAsync task completes and calls MoveNext again. The switch on state jumps to the right spot.
  • 6. At the end builder.SetResult(a + b) completes the task. If an exception was thrown, it's builder.SetException.
cards/1/task: The responses are still on their way. Step through MoveNext and count the calls and pauses.
cards/2/q: A method has two awaits, and neither task is ready yet. How many times is MoveNext called?
cards/2/explain: builder.Start makes the first call, then there's one more for each continuation after an await.
cards/3/q: Why isn't variable a lost between MoveNext calls?
cards/3/options/0: It became a field of the state machine
cards/3/options/1: The thread that started the method keeps it
cards/3/explain: The stack frame disappears between MoveNext calls, but the struct's fields stay. The thread has nothing to do with it: a different thread may run the continuation.
cards/4/q: Who calls MoveNext the first time, and on which thread?
cards/4/options/0: builder.Start, synchronously, on the thread that called the method
cards/4/options/1: The thread pool, right after the method is called
cards/4/options/2: The GetAAsync task, when it completes
cards/4/explain: The first MoveNext runs right inside the method call. The GetAAsync task calls MoveNext the second time, after the pause.
cards/5/task: Turn on "Results are ready" and walk through again.
cards/6/q: By the time of the await, both tasks, GetAAsync and GetBAsync, have already completed. How many pauses and MoveNext calls are there?
cards/6/explain: IsCompleted = true, so the subscribe branch is skipped and the method runs straight through in the first MoveNext call, the one builder.Start made.
cards/7/title: On the stack, then on the heap
cards/7/body: In Release the state machine is a struct and lives on the stack as long as the method hasn't suspended. At the first real pause the builder moves it to the heap: it has to outlive the method's return, because MoveNext will be called later.
cards/7/deep: In .NET Core 2.1+ the state machine's "box" is the task itself: AsyncStateMachineBox derives from Task<T>, so a pause costs a single allocation. In Debug the machine is a class so that Edit and Continue works.
cards/8/q: MoveNext hit an awaiter that isn't done. Put its actions in order.
cards/8/items/1: Writes the step number to state
cards/8/items/2: Subscribes MoveNext to completion via builder.AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted
cards/8/explain: state is written before subscribing: the continuation may start on another thread right after the subscription, and the switch must see the correct step number.
cards/9/q: Match each part of the state machine to its role
cards/9/pairs/0/1: The step number where it stopped
cards/9/pairs/1/1: Runs a piece of the method up to the next await
